payload:
SELECT Account.id as "AccountID", Account.name, Account.accountnumber, Account.batch,  Account.additionalemailaddresses, 
contact.firstname, contact.lastname, contact.workemail, contact.personalemail, 
Invoice.amount, Invoice.balance, Invoice.duedate, Invoice.invoicedate, Invoice.invoicenumber, 
Invoice.status, Invoice.id,
date_diff('day', Invoice.duedate, current_date)  as "duedays",
Subscription.id as "SubscriptionID", Subscription.name, Subscription.status 
FROM InvoiceItem IT
JOIN Account on IT.accountid = Account.id
JOIN Invoice on IT.invoiceid = Invoice.id
JOIN contact  on contact.id = Account.BillToId
JOIN Subscription on IT.subscriptionid = Subscription.id
WHERE (date_diff('day', invoice.duedate, current_date) = CAST(CAST('{{Data.Workflow.a}}' AS BOOLEAN) AS BIGINT)
OR date_diff('day', invoice.duedate, current_date) = CAST(CAST('{{Data.Workflow.b}}' AS BOOLEAN) AS BIGINT)
OR date_diff('day', invoice.duedate, current_date) = CAST(CAST('{{Data.Workflow.c}}' AS BOOLEAN) AS BIGINT)
OR date_diff('day', invoice.duedate, current_date) = CAST(CAST('{{Data.Workflow.d}}' AS BOOLEAN) AS BIGINT)
OR date_diff('day', invoice.duedate, current_date) = CAST(CAST('{{Data.Workflow.e}}' AS BOOLEAN) AS BIGINT)) 
AND Invoice.balance>0 
AND Invoice.status = 'Posted' 
AND Account.Batch = 'Batch1'

payload:
3.2. Metabolite sets and metabolic pathways altered by PQ
Following DMs screening, we performed metabolite set enrichment analysis and KEGG pathway analysis to identify the effect of PQ exposure on metabolite sets and pathways. The enrichment analysis results revealed that PQ predominantly altered amino acids and peptides in both the endo- and exo- metabolome (Fig. 2 A, B). Pathway analysis showed that intracellular DMs were enriched in 14 pathways (Table S1), while extracellular DMs in 12 pathways (Table S2). To expand our analysis to include more metabolic pathways, we screened the main affected metabolic pathways and integrated the intracellular and extracellular screening results (Fig. 2 C, D; Table S3). Among these, amino acid metabolism, including phenylalanine and tyrosine metabolism, arginine metabolism, tryptophan metabolism and histidine metabolism, were mainly altered under PQ exposure. Additionally, PQ also interfered with pyrimidine metabolism, galactose metabolism, vitamin B6 metabolism and lysine degradation. These analyses strongly indicated that amino acid metabolism dysregulation could be an important mechanism of PQ toxicity on mNSCs.

Furthermore, to identify the different patterns of metabolic dysregulation in response to different doses of PQ, we also conducted metabolite set and pathway enrichment analyses for the unique DMs identified in each treated group (Fig. 1 G, H) (19, 95, 70 intracellular DMs for 10, 20, 40 μM PQ treated groups, and 120, 95, 23 extracellular DMs for 10, 20, 40 μM PQ treated groups). The main affected metabolic pathways of each group were also listed in Table S5 with the DMs enriched. We found that amino acid metabolism and nucleotide metabolism was significantly changed by 20 and 40 μM PQ, while 10 μM PQ induced very few metabolic perturbations (Fig. S1, S2). Interestingly, energy metabolism, including pyruvate metabolism, Glycolysis / Gluconeogenesis and TCA cycle, was only significantly enriched in 20 μM PQ treated group (Fig. S2 C). This might suggest a unique toxicity mechanism of PQ at dose of 20 μM.

The problems with higher education. The six biggest problems with American higher education are as follows. Colleges are too expensive and inefficient. Student fees are high. It costs three times as much to go to college as it did, say, 30 years ago.

Students don't work very hard and learn little. Several surveys independently confirm that the typical full-time undergraduate spends less than 30 hours weekly on studies, less than on recreational activities.

There is a lack of information on which to evaluate the effectiveness of universities. Colleges don't even know whether their seniors know more than their freshmen. Information on finances is often largely hidden as well. How can you evaluate their efficiency or success if you do not have basic information?

The minority of students graduate on time, and many don't graduate at all. Just 36 percent of students entering bachelor's degree programs graduate within the four years that a degree is supposed to take. Well over 40 percent do not graduate within six years. There are big schools with low graduation rates. Why accredit these institutions?

There is a gap between enrollment levels and student curricula on the one hand and needs of the American labor market on the other. We have great numbers of college-educated taxi drivers, barmen, waiters, beauticians, and so forth. A fellow with a master's degree cutting grass is not uncommon.

Federal student financial aid policies have been a failure. Federal grants are a disaster. They were designed to help low income kids go to college. The aid programs do not reward good academic performance more than bad, and have contributed to a lowering of higher education.
